about: The scripted AI lesson for p3-particle-model (2026-11-17, Phase B, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-15-script-four-topics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p1-energy-stores.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about solids, liquids and gases: what they are made of, and why each one behaves as it does.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from the energy lessons. A ball rolls across the floor. Which of its energy stores is filled by its movement?
steps.right: Yes: a moving object has energy in its kinetic store.

wrong.other: Not quite: kinetic, the store for moving things.
wrong.chem: Not quite: the chemical store is in fuels and food. A moving ball has energy in its kinetic store.
wrong.elastic: Not quite: nothing is stretched or squashed. A moving ball has energy in its kinetic store.

idk.hint: The kinetic store is for moving things, the chemical store for fuels and food, the elastic potential store for stretched things. Which fits a rolling ball?

steps.answerWhy: A moving object has energy in its kinetic store.

steps.question: Second: a hot cup of tea cools down on the table. Which energy store of the tea empties as it cools?
steps.right: Yes: as the tea cools, energy leaves its thermal store and warms the surroundings.

wrong.other: Not quite: thermal, the store for how hot something is.
wrong.kinetic: Not quite: the cup of tea is not moving across the table. Energy leaves its thermal store as it cools.
wrong.chem: Not quite: nothing burns. Energy leaves the tea's thermal store as it cools.

idk.hint: The thermal store is the one for how hot something is. Which button is that?

steps.answerWhy: Energy leaves the tea's thermal store as it cools, warming the surroundings.

steps.text: Now this lesson. Everything around you is made of tiny particles, far too small to see, and they never stop moving.
Matter comes in three states: solid, liquid and gas. Ice, water and steam are one substance in its three states. The particles stay the same; only their arrangement and movement change.
In a solid, the particles are packed close together in a regular pattern called a lattice. Strong forces of attraction between the particles hold each one in its place.
A solid's particles cannot swap places, but they are not still: each one vibrates, jiggling to and fro about a fixed position.

steps.question: Why does an ice cube keep its shape?

options.text: Strong forces hold each particle in its place

steps.right: Yes: each particle is held in its place in the lattice, so the whole solid keeps its shape.

wrong.other: Not quite: strong forces hold each particle in its place.
wrong.still: Not quite: the particles are never still: they vibrate. They stay in shape because strong forces hold each one in its place.
wrong.gas: Not quite: solid particles are close together. Strong forces hold each one in its place, so the shape stays.

idk.hint: Can a particle in a solid move to a new place? What stops it?

steps.answerWhy: Strong forces of attraction hold each particle in its place, so a solid keeps its shape.

steps.text: A solid also has a fixed volume: the amount of space it takes up does not change.
A solid is incompressible: you cannot squash it into a smaller space, because its particles are already touching.
In a liquid, the particles touch each other too, but they are jumbled, with no pattern. The forces between them are weaker, so they can slide past each other.
A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, but its volume stays fixed. You cannot squash a liquid much either.

steps.question: Which state has particles that touch but can slide past each other?
steps.right: Yes: a liquid. Its particles touch but can move past each other, so it flows.

wrong.solid: Not quite: in a solid the particles only vibrate in place; they cannot slide past each other. That is a liquid.
wrong.gas: Not quite: gas particles are far apart. Touching but sliding past each other is a liquid.

idk.hint: Which state flows but keeps its volume?

steps.answerWhy: In a liquid the particles touch but can slide past each other.

steps.text: In a gas, the particles are far apart and move fast in random directions. The forces between them are almost zero.
A gas has no fixed shape or volume: it spreads out to fill any container. Most of a gas is empty space, so you can squash it into a smaller volume.
Air is a gas, made of particles. Between those particles there is nothing at all: just empty space.
The picture shows the three states side by side. Notice that each particle is drawn the same size in all three.

steps.question: A syringe is sealed at the end. You can push the plunger in when it holds air, but not when it holds water. Why?

options.text: Air particles are far apart, with empty space between them
Air particles are smaller and softer than water particles
Water particles are too heavy to move

steps.right: Yes: the air particles have empty space between them to close up. Water particles are already touching.

wrong.other: Not quite: air particles are far apart, with empty space between them; water particles are touching.
wrong.soft: Not quite: size and softness are not the reason. Air particles are far apart, so there is space to close up; water particles already touch.
wrong.heavy: Not quite: weight is not the reason. Water particles are already touching, while air particles have empty space between them.

idk.hint: Think about the gaps between the particles in a gas and in a liquid.

steps.answerWhy: Gas particles are far apart, with empty space to close up; liquid particles are already touching.

steps.prompt: In one line: how are the particles arranged in a solid, and how do they move?
points: close together in a regular pattern
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: in a solid the particles are close together in a regular pattern, and they vibrate about fixed positions.

keyPoints.heading: Internal energy and the particle model

steps.text: The particles in a substance have energy in two ways. Because they move, they have kinetic energy: the energy of movement.
Particles also attract each other. Because of these forces of attraction, particles have potential energy: energy stored by the forces between them.
The internal energy of a substance is the total kinetic and potential energy of all its particles.
Heating a substance raises its internal energy, in one of two ways.
First way: the particles move faster, so their kinetic energy rises. A thermometer shows this as a rise in temperature: the hotter something is, the faster its particles move on average.
Faster particles also push each other a little further apart, which is why most things expand, getting slightly bigger, when they are heated.

steps.question: A cup of water and a bath of water are both at 20 °C. Which has more internal energy?

options.text: The bath: it has far more particles
Neither: they are at the same temperature
The cup: its particles are closer together

steps.right: Yes: the particles in both move at the same average speed, but the bath has far more of them, so far more internal energy.

wrong.other: Not quite: the bath, because it has far more particles.
wrong.same: Not quite: the same temperature means the same average speed for each particle, not the same total. The bath has far more particles, so far more internal energy.
wrong.cup: Not quite: the particles are just as close in both. The bath has far more particles, so far more internal energy.

idk.hint: Internal energy adds up the energy of every particle. Which has more particles?

steps.answerWhy: Internal energy is the total for all the particles, and the bath has far more particles.

steps.text: Second way: the substance melts or boils. The energy overcomes some of the forces holding the particles in place, so their potential energy rises while the temperature stays the same.

steps.question: Water is boiling in a pan at 100 °C, and its temperature is not rising. What is the energy from the hob doing?
steps.right: Yes: the energy overcomes the forces between the particles, so their potential energy rises. Their kinetic energy, and the temperature, stay the same.

wrong.other: Not quite: it raises the particles' potential energy.
wrong.faster: Not quite: if the particles moved faster, the temperature would rise. The energy overcomes the forces between them, raising their potential energy.
wrong.lost: Not quite: energy is never lost. It overcomes the forces between the particles, raising their potential energy, so the internal energy rises.

idk.hint: The temperature is steady, so the particles are not speeding up. Which kind of energy is left?

steps.answerWhy: The temperature is steady, so the kinetic energy is not changing; the energy raises the particles' potential energy.

steps.question: Water in a pan is heated from 20 °C to 60 °C. Which energy of its particles rises?
steps.right: Yes: the temperature rises, so the particles move faster and their kinetic energy rises.

wrong.pot: Not quite: the water does not boil here; its temperature rises. Rising temperature means faster particles: more kinetic energy.
wrong.none: Not quite: energy is going in and the temperature rises, so the particles' kinetic energy rises.

idk.hint: Does the temperature change here? Which energy goes with temperature?

steps.answerWhy: The temperature rises, so the particles move faster: their kinetic energy rises.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is internal energy?
points: the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a substance.

steps.text: Changing from one state to another is called a change of state. Melting is solid to liquid, and freezing is liquid back to solid.
The temperature at which a solid turns to liquid is its melting point. A liquid freezes at that same temperature: for water, both happen at 0 °C.
Boiling turns a liquid into a gas all through the liquid, with bubbles of gas forming inside it. Boiling happens at one temperature, the boiling point: 100 °C for water.
Evaporation also turns a liquid into a gas, but only at its surface, and at any temperature. The fastest particles escape from the surface, which is why wet washing dries.
Condensing is a gas turning back into a liquid, like steam misting a cold window.
Sublimation is a solid turning straight into a gas. Dry ice, which is solid carbon dioxide, does this at room temperature.
Freezing and condensing are the reverse of melting and boiling: the forces pull the particles back together, the particles lose potential energy, and energy comes out.
The picture shows all six changes. Going right needs energy in; going left gives energy out.

steps.question: A puddle dries up on a cold day, without ever getting near 100 °C. Which change of state is this?
steps.right: Yes: evaporation. Water escapes from the puddle's surface even when it is cold.

wrong.boil: Not quite: boiling needs the water to reach 100 °C, all through it. Liquid escaping from the surface at a low temperature is evaporation.
wrong.cond: Not quite: condensing is gas turning into liquid. The puddle turns from liquid into gas: evaporation.

idk.hint: The water leaves from the surface of the puddle at a low temperature. Is that boiling?

steps.answerWhy: Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid at any temperature; boiling happens all through it at the boiling point.

steps.question: 100 g of ice melts completely in a sealed bag. Predict: what is the mass of the water?

wrong.less: Not quite: nothing escapes from the sealed bag, so the water is still 100 g.
wrong.more: Not quite: nothing is added to the bag, so the water is still 100 g.

idk.hint: Is anything added to the sealed bag, or taken out?

steps.answerWhy: Nothing enters or leaves the sealed bag, so the water is still 100 g.

steps.text: In every change of state the mass stays the same, because the number of particles does not change.
Changes of state are physical changes: reverse one and the substance gets back its original properties, as melted chocolate sets again as chocolate.
A chemical change makes new substances, so it cannot be undone that way: ash cannot be turned back into wood.

steps.question: Which of these is a physical change?
steps.right: Yes: cool the melted butter and it sets as butter again.

wrong.bake: Not quite: baking makes new substances, so it is a chemical change. Butter melting is physical: cool it and it sets again.
wrong.rust: Not quite: rust is a new substance, so rusting is a chemical change. Butter melting is physical.

idk.hint: Which one can you undo, to get the same substance back?

steps.answerWhy: Melting is a change of state, so it is physical: cooled butter sets as butter again.

steps.text: To find what state a substance is in, compare the temperature with its melting and boiling points. Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C, so at 20 °C, between the two, it is a liquid.

steps.question: Ethanol, the alcohol in hand gel, melts at −114 °C and boils at 78 °C. What state is it in at 20 °C?
steps.right: Yes: 20 °C is above its melting point but below its boiling point, so it is a liquid.

wrong.solid: Not quite: 20 °C is far above its melting point of −114 °C, so it has melted. It is below its boiling point, so it is a liquid.
wrong.gas: Not quite: 20 °C is below its boiling point of 78 °C, so it has not boiled. It is a liquid.

idk.hint: Is 20 °C above or below each of the two temperatures?

steps.answerWhy: 20 °C is above the melting point and below the boiling point, so ethanol is a liquid.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is the difference between evaporation and boiling?
points: evaporation happens only at the surface, at any temperature
boiling happens all through the liquid, at the boiling point
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: evaporation happens only at the surface, at any temperature; boiling happens all through the liquid, at the boiling point.

steps.text: Everything in this lesson so far is a model: a simple picture of what we cannot see, used to explain and predict. This one is called the particle model.
The particle model explains a lot: why a gas is easy to squash, why a solid keeps its shape, and why a gas presses on its container: its particles keep hitting the walls.
Diffusion is explained too: particles moving at random spread out from where there are many to where there are few. A smell spreads across a room in this way.
But a model is not the real thing. The particle model draws every particle as a solid ball, and all the particles of a substance as identical.
Real particles come in different sizes and shapes, and they are not hard little balls.

steps.question: A textbook draws the particles of a gas about two particle-widths apart. What is wrong with the drawing?

options.text: Real gas particles are much further apart than that
Gas particles should be in a regular pattern

steps.right: Yes: drawings are not to scale. In a real gas the gaps are far bigger than any page can show.

wrong.other: Not quite: real gas particles are much further apart than that.
wrong.touch: Not quite: touching particles are a solid or a liquid. Real gas particles are much further apart than any drawing shows.
wrong.pattern: Not quite: a regular pattern is a solid. Real gas particles are far apart, much further than any drawing shows.

idk.hint: Most of a gas is empty space. Does a drawing with small gaps show that?

steps.answerWhy: Particle drawings are not to scale: real gas particles are much further apart than they can be drawn.

steps.prompt: In one line: name one thing the particle model explains, and one way real particles differ from its pictures.
points: something it explains (squashing a gas, gas pressure, diffusion, a solid keeping its shape)
real particles are not identical solid balls, or the pictures are not to scale
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the particle model explains why a gas can be squashed, but real particles are not identical solid balls.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: which state has particles far apart, moving fast in random directions?

wrong.other: Not quite: a gas. Its particles are far apart and move fast in random directions.
wrong.w1: Not quite: liquid particles touch each other. Far apart and fast is a gas.
wrong.w2: Not quite: solid particles are close together and vibrate in place. Far apart and fast is a gas.

steps.answerWhy: In a gas the particles are far apart and move fast in random directions.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: what is internal energy?

options.text: The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles
The kinetic energy of one particle

steps.right: Yes: the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles.

wrong.other: Not quite: it is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles.
wrong.w1: Not quite: temperature is linked to the particles' kinetic energy. Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles.
wrong.w2: Not quite: it adds up all the particles, and their potential energy too.

steps.answerWhy: Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: while ice melts at 0 °C, which is true of its temperature?
steps.right: Yes: it stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted.

wrong.other: Not quite: it stays at 0 °C while the ice melts.
wrong.w1: Not quite: the energy raises the particles' potential energy, not their kinetic energy, so the temperature stays at 0 °C.
wrong.w2: Not quite: energy is going in, and the temperature stays at 0 °C while it melts.

steps.answerWhy: While a substance changes state its temperature stays the same.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: a 50 g block of wax melts. What is the mass of the liquid wax?
steps.right: Yes: 50 g. Mass stays the same in a change of state.

wrong.w1: Not quite: 50 g. No particles are lost when wax melts, so the mass stays the same.
wrong.w2: Not quite: 50 g. No particles are added when wax melts, so the mass stays the same.

steps.answerWhy: Mass stays the same in a change of state, so the liquid wax is 50 g.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: which change turns a solid straight into a gas?

wrong.w1: Not quite: melting turns a solid into a liquid. Solid straight to gas is sublimation.
wrong.w2: Not quite: condensing is gas to liquid. Solid straight to gas is sublimation.

steps.answerWhy: Sublimation turns a solid straight into a gas, as dry ice does.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: mercury melts at −39 °C and boils at 357 °C. What state is it in at 400 °C?
steps.right: Yes: 400 °C is above its boiling point, so it is a gas.

wrong.other: Not quite: a gas. 400 °C is above its boiling point of 357 °C.
wrong.w1: Not quite: 400 °C is above its boiling point of 357 °C, so it has boiled: it is a gas.
wrong.w2: Not quite: 400 °C is far above both temperatures, so it is a gas.

steps.answerWhy: 400 °C is above mercury's boiling point of 357 °C, so it is a gas.

steps.text: That's the end of the quiz: you got {right} out of {n}.
